title: Krishna Argues for Worshipping Govardhana Hill
story:
Nanda had explained the great sacrifice to his son: it belonged to Indra, the lord of rain, and the cowherds of Vrindavan had offered it to him every season for as long as anyone could remember. Krishna listened to his father. Then he spoke — and he spoke against giving the sacrifice to Indra.

He began where, in his telling, everything begins and ends: with what a person does. Every being is born by its own actions, he said, and by its own actions it comes to its end. Joy and sorrow, fear and safety — all of it is reached through what one has done. And if some lord hands out the fruits of other people's deeds, that lord only follows the one who acts; he has no power over one who has done nothing. So what need is there of Indra, when every creature is simply walking the road its own nature has laid down?

The cows, he said, were the point. Look at how this village lives. You are not farmers tied to a plot of soil, nor merchants counting their goods. Of all the ways a man may earn his bread — tilling the earth, trading, tending cattle, lending — yours has always been the cattle. The herd is your whole wealth and your whole work, and the herd does not live on Indra's favour. It lives on grass and water and the shelter of the hills.

The clouds do pour down rain, he allowed. But they do not rain because a king in heaven commands them. It is their own nature that moves them, and by that rain every creature thrives. What, then, has the great Indra to do with it?

And there was more. A man should honour the very thing by which he lives, for whoever thrives by one thing and bows to another finds no safety in it; whoever is helped by one and worships another, he said, meets calamity both in this world and in the next. He said it plainly, with an image the village would not forget, comparing such a man to a faithless wife who leaves her own home for strangers and in the end keeps nothing.

We have no cities, he reminded them — no towns, no walled houses. We are people of the forest, and we have always lived among forests and hills. So let the hills be honoured, and the cows that feed us, and the brahmins who bless us. Let the sacrifice be for them.

He told them exactly how to do it. Let them take the very offerings they had gathered for Indra — the grain, the milk, the fuel, the gifts — and give them instead to the hill. Let them cook the rich dishes and the milk-rice. Let the brahmins feed the fires. Let food be set before every guest, even the lowliest, and fodder before the cows, and the offering before the hill itself. Then, washed and dressed and fed, let them walk in a circle around the cows, the brahmins, the fire, and the mountain.

"This is my thought, father," he said. "Do it, if it pleases you. This sacrifice, to the cows, the brahmins, and the hills, is dear to me."

He did not say all that was in his mind. Indra's pride had grown too great, and Krishna meant to humble it — but he did not speak of that to Nanda. He spoke of grass and rain and the shape of a cowherd's life, and he made it sound like the plainest common sense in the world.

And so it must have seemed to the men who heard him, because they agreed to do exactly as he said.
reflection: Krishna's argument is striking because he does not attack ritual itself. He redirects it to the things that actually sustain the cowherds, grass and water and the hill and the herd, and asks them to honour the source of their own living rather than a distant king of heaven.
tradition_note: The Harivamsha (1.70) and the Vishnu Purana (5.10) give the same argument in nearly the same words, the cowherds reasoning that cattle are their livelihood and the forest their home, so the cow, the mountain, and the forest should receive the offering rather than Indra.
next_story_tease: And so the cowherds took the offerings meant for Indra and carried them to the hill, where something wonderful was waiting for them.
hero_scene: Krishna speaking earnestly to the cowherd elders, gesturing toward Govardhana hill and the grazing cattle, arguing that the hill and the cows, not Indra, deserve the sacrifice.
visual_elements: Nanda and the cowherd elders listening
